candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9999 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with SHAP contributions from +0.0063 to +0.0169. That is a strong statistical signal, but the listed evidence is not specific enough to confirm cryptojacking. Every n-gram is a short two-instruction mnemonic pair that is common in compiled x86 code: CMOVZ MOV, ADD POP, XOR CALL, TEST JZ, CALL ADD, PUSH SUB, MOV JZ, LEA CALL, SUB MOV and MOV LEA. The reported frequencies are all 0.000000, so no pattern is visibly concentrated in the binary. No function names or locations are listed, so none of the patterns can be tied to a specific routine such as a hashing loop or a mining routine. The only patterns that loosely suggest bitwise or arithmetic mixing are XOR XOR (+0.008826), XOR SHL (+0.007046), XOR MOV (+0.009663) and AND MOV (+0.008101). Even these are generic and appear in many non-mining programs. The CMOVZ and CMOVNZ patterns (CMOVZ MOV, XOR CMOVNZ, CMP CMOVZ) hint at branchless conditional logic, but that is not specific to mining either. The contributions are also spread fairly evenly, with no single dominant indicator. The classifier's confidence is therefore not matched by interpretable, behavior-specific evidence, which supports a low-confidence tier. Malicious classification is plausible and warrants follow-up.
